summary: Offers advice to designers of link-layer protocols and equipment that use Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ), who may not know the Internet's architecture. It explains how design choices affect the performance and efficiency of Internet traffic. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If a link resends lost data on its own, it can help or hurt the traffic sitting on top. This document gives tips so link builders resend in a way that helps.

questions: how does link layer retransmission affect tcp
should link layers retransmit lost frames
how does link arq affect tcp
subtitle: How far should a link keep resending lost frames before it gives up? Advice for people who design links.

tldr.problem: Link designers add Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) so lossy links resend damaged frames, but they may not realise how that extra delay, jitter and reordering affects TCP, UDP and other Internet traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the two common ARQ styles, defines perfect, high and low persistence, and discusses packet ordering, multiple flows and separate link service classes.
tldr.outcome: When a link cannot tell flows apart, low persistence and preserved packet ordering are generally best. Perfect or extremely high persistence is generally undesirable.

today: RFC 3366 is a Best Current Practice document, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is advice rather than a protocol, and it says there is insufficient experience to recommend a specific ARQ scheme for any class of link.

sections.title: Who This Advice Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3366 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 62) written for people who design digital communication equipment and link-layer protocols that use link-layer ARQ. It assumes they want to carry Internet protocols but may not know the Internet's architecture or how their choices affect traffic.

It names three audiences: link designers tuning a link with standard mechanisms such as HDLC, implementers designing new link mechanisms, and TCP and UDP developers who want to know how links can behave. Perfect reliability is not a requirement for IP networks. Packets can be discarded for reasons unrelated to channel errors, and perfect end-to-end reliability can be ensured only at or above the transport layer.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guidebook for people who build the wires and radio links the Internet runs on. It helps them avoid accidentally making things slower.

sections.title: Link ARQ and Why Use It
sections.content:
At the link layer, ARQ works on frames, which are often small and of fixed or maximum size, unlike variable-length IP packets. It relies on an integrity check for each frame, such as a strong link-layer CRC, to detect errors, and retransmits frames that are missing or corrupted. A frame may carry all or part of one or more IP packets.

The RFC lists causes of loss on a link: channel noise, interference and link outages, plus shared-channel collisions, congestion discards and implementation errors. It gives two reasons to use ARQ. A single-link control loop is faster than TCP's end-to-end acknowledgement loop, and small frames let the link repeat just the damaged part of a packet. Forward Error Correction (FEC) and Hybrid ARQ are mentioned as complementary techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can notice a smudged page and quickly ask for a fresh copy, much faster than waiting for the final reader to complain from the other end of the road.

sections.title: Stop-and-Wait and Sliding-Window ARQ
sections.content:
Two ARQ styles are widely used. With stop-and-wait ARQ (also called Idle ARQ) the sender transmits one frame and waits for its acknowledgement. It is simple but inefficient, and on a link it suits only low bandwidth-delay products, so the RFC does not discuss it further.

With sliding-window ARQ every frame has a sequence number, counted modulo a fixed base. The sender may have several frames outstanding, up to its window. A window at least as large as the link's bandwidth*delay product permits continuous transmission. The sequence space must be larger than the window, and larger than twice the window for selective repeat. Selective Repeat (SREJ) and Go-Back-N (REJ) are examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Stop-and-wait is like asking after every single word whether you were heard. Sliding window is like sending a whole sentence and only repeating the words the listener missed.

sections.title: Where Delay Comes From
sections.content:
Links add to the total path delay in several ways: queuing and buffering at the link head, retransmission back-off on shared channels, waiting for channel access, frame serialisation, propagation time, per-frame processing (QoS scheduling, encryption, FEC, interleaving) and reassembly at the receiver. Every retransmission can repeat most of these steps.

Applications and transport protocols only see the overall path delay, not the delay of each link, and the path may contain an arbitrary number of links that may or may not use ARQ. So the RFC says it is not possible to state fixed limits on the acceptable delay that one link can add.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stop on a bus route adds a little waiting time, and the passenger only knows the total. So every stop should be quick.

sections.title: ARQ Persistence
sections.content:
Persistence is the willingness of an ARQ protocol to keep retransmitting lost frames. It defines how long a link may delay a packet while trying to send all its frames before giving up and discarding it. It is normally measured in milliseconds, or as a maximum number of retransmission attempts.

  • Perfectly persistent protocols, such as ISO HDLC in Asynchronous Balanced Mode and LAP-B, retransmit an indefinite number of times. The RFC argues against this for IP: it adds jitter, gives no upper bound on delay, can trigger TCP timeouts, and duplicates what end hosts already do. Truly unlimited ARQ is seldom found in real implementations.
  • High-persistence protocols cap the number of attempts but can still delay packets for a long time. The RFC recalls that a packet should never be delayed more than TCP's Maximum Segment Lifetime of 120 seconds.
  • Low-persistence protocols accept that they will discard some frames, which bounds added delay (typically below the TCP path RTO) and stops one lost frame from blocking other complete packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Perfect persistence is a friend who will never stop knocking on a locked door. Low persistence knocks a few times and moves on so everyone else is not kept waiting.

sections.title: Choosing Persistence and Handling Outages
sections.content:
A lower link persistence, of the order of 2 to 5 retransmission attempts, reduces interaction with the TCP RTO timer. A link with very low propagation delay may allow tens of attempts and still be fine, provided the total packet transmission time stays much less than 100 ms. Delay accumulates along a path, which is an argument for lower persistence on each individual link.

During a transient outage longer than the TCP RTO, the TCP sender retransmits, reduces its congestion window to 1 segment and waits for an ACK. If the link has discarded that ACK, TCP learns the link is back only at its next RTO retransmission, which can be many seconds later. Longer persistence combined with separate service classes might help, but the RFC calls such schemes a research issue. On shared channels, uncontrolled high persistence can consume capacity that other nodes could use.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road is closed for a while, the delivery driver should not circle the block forever. A few tries, then let the sender try again later.

sections.title: Packet Ordering, Flows and Service Classes
sections.content:
IP networks are not required to deliver packets in order. Significant reordering within a flow is still undesirable. It raises jitter for real-time applications and creates duplicate ACKs, and three identical duplicate ACKs make a TCP sender start fast retransmission. Ideally the link should not add to reordering within a flow, which needs buffering at the link receiver. Reordering between different flows can be desirable for fair sharing.

When several flows share a link, ARQ for one flow's loss can add jitter to others, including UDP flows that did not want reliable delivery. Separate link service classes would help, but the link needs an explicit indication of each flow's class. The RFC lists the IP Type of Service or diffserv DSCP bits, the IP protocol type, and TCP or UDP port numbers, and notes the drawbacks of each (values overwritten along the path, tunnelling, NAT, IPSec ESP encryption, IPv6 header parsing). Approach (a), using the ToS and DSCP bits, may be beneficial and is preferable to inspecting packet contents. If flows cannot be told apart, all flows should get the same behaviour and a low persistency is best.
sections.plainLanguage: Shuffling the order of pages in a book makes it hard to read, but letting a short letter overtake a huge parcel can be fair, as long as each letter's own pages stay in order.

sections.title: Conclusions and Security
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that when links cannot classify flows and treat them separately, low persistence is generally desirable and preserving packet ordering is generally desirable. Extremely high and perfect persistence are generally undesirable; high persistence is a bad idea unless flow classification and accurate knowledge of flow requirements make it beneficial. There is insufficient experience to recommend a specific ARQ scheme for any class of link, and ARQ is only one method of error recovery alongside rate adaptation, power adaptation, adaptive modulation, FEC and interleaving.

On security, no implications for IP traffic were identified, but an unreliable link may hurt link-layer key management protocols, and attacks that exploit a link's retransmission behaviour and propagation delay could cause a form of jamming. No IANA assignments are required.
sections.plainLanguage: When in doubt, try only a few times and keep things in order. Never promise to keep trying forever.
